blocks.body:
Among all triangles with perimeter $12$, which has the largest area? How far can a point inside a triangle be from the vertices compared with its distance from the sides? Can a fence of length $L$ enclose more than $L^2/(4\pi)$? Questions like these compare lengths, areas and angles of figures, and they have two kinds of answer: an inequality, and a description of the shapes where it is sharp.

This lesson works through the standard toolkit for such problems and proves three landmark results at the reader's level: Euler's inequality $R\ge2r$, the Erdős–Mordell inequality, and the isoperimetric inequality for triangles, together with the statement of the full isoperimetric inequality $4\pi A\le L^2$.

blocks.title: The toolkit
Euler's inequality
blocks.body: For every triangle, $R\ge2r$, with equality if and only if the triangle is equilateral.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
From $A=\dfrac{abc}{4R}$ and $A=rs$ we get $R=\dfrac{abc}{4A}$ and $r=\dfrac As$, so

$$R\ge2r\iff\frac{abc}{4A}\ge\frac{2A}{s}\iff abc\,s\ge8A^2=8\,s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)\iff abc\ge8(s-a)(s-b)(s-c).$$

In Ravi variables this reads $(y+z)(z+x)(x+y)\ge8xyz$. By AM–GM, $y+z\ge2\sqrt{yz}$, $z+x\ge2\sqrt{zx}$ and $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}$; multiplying the three gives the claim. Equality needs $x=y=z$, that is $a=b=c$.

A sharper fact, also due to Euler, is the distance formula $OI^2=R(R-2r)$ between circumcentre and incentre; it implies the inequality at once, but its proof takes more work and we do not need it.

blocks.title: The Erdős–Mordell inequality
blocks.body:
Let $P$ be a point inside or on the boundary of triangle $ABC$, and let $D,E,F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$. Then

$$PA+PB+PC\ge2\,(PD+PE+PF).$$

Equality holds if and only if the triangle is equilateral and $P$ is its centre.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Step 1: $a\cdot PA\ge c\cdot PE+b\cdot PF$. If $P=A$ both sides are $0$. Otherwise let $P'$ be the reflection of $P$ in the bisector of angle $A$. The reflection fixes $A$ and swaps the lines $AB$ and $AC$, so $AP'=AP$, the distance from $P'$ to $AB$ is $PE$, and the distance from $P'$ to $AC$ is $PF$. It also maps the angular region $BAC$ onto itself, so $P'$ lies in it and the ray $AP'$ meets segment $BC$ at some point $K$. The distances from $B$ and $C$ to the line $AK$ are at most $BK$ and $CK$, so they add up to at most $BK+KC=a$. Now compute the areas of triangles $ABP'$ and $AP'C$ twice, once with bases $AB$ and $AC$ and once with the common base $AP'$:

$$c\cdot PE+b\cdot PF=2[ABP']+2[AP'C]=AP'\cdot\big(d(B,AK)+d(C,AK)\big)\le a\cdot PA.$$

Step 2: in the same way, $b\cdot PB\ge c\cdot PD+a\cdot PF$ and $c\cdot PC\ge b\cdot PD+a\cdot PE$ (each time: the length of a side at the vertex, times the distance to the other side at that vertex).

Step 3: divide by $a$, $b$, $c$ respectively and add:

$$PA+PB+PC\ge\Big(\frac cb+\frac bc\Big)PD+\Big(\frac ca+\frac ac\Big)PE+\Big(\frac ba+\frac ab\Big)PF\ge2(PD+PE+PF),$$

since $t+\frac1t\ge2$ for $t>0$.

Equality: for an interior point all three distances are positive, so equality in Step 3 forces $a=b=c$. Equality in Step 1 forces $d(B,AK)=BK$ and $d(C,AK)=CK$, so $AK\perp BC$; in an equilateral triangle this line is the bisector at $A$, so $P'$, and hence $P$, lies on it. Doing this at every vertex puts $P$ at the centre. A similar check shows that equality never occurs for a point on the boundary.

blocks.title: The isoperimetric inequality
blocks.body:
The isoperimetric problem asks for the closed curve of given length $L$ enclosing the largest area $A$. The answer, the circle, has been believed since antiquity; complete proofs came only in the nineteenth century, and a short one came from Hurwitz in 1902 using Fourier series. The statement is:

For every simple closed curve of length $L$ bounding a region of area $A$, $4\pi A\le L^2$, with equality only for the circle.

We do not prove this here (it needs either analysis beyond our prerequisites or a careful existence argument), but its polygon versions are within reach. For a regular $n$-gon with inradius $\rho$, each side is $2\rho\tan(\pi/n)$, so $L=2n\rho\tan(\pi/n)$ and $A=\tfrac12L\rho=n\rho^2\tan(\pi/n)$. Hence

$$\frac{L^2}{A}=4n\tan\frac\pi n,$$

which is $12\sqrt3\approx20.78$ for the triangle, $16$ for the square, and decreases towards $4\pi\approx12.57$ as $n$ grows (because $\tan t>t$ for $0< t< \pi/2$, it always stays above $4\pi$). Regular polygons with more sides are more efficient, and the circle is the limit.

blocks.title: Isoperimetric inequality for triangles
blocks.body: Among all triangles with perimeter $L=2s$, the equilateral one has the largest area: $A\le\dfrac{s^2}{3\sqrt3}=\dfrac{L^2}{12\sqrt3}$, with equality only for the equilateral triangle.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: In Ravi variables $x+y+z=s$ and $A^2=s\,xyz$. By AM–GM, $xyz\le\left(\tfrac{x+y+z}3\right)^3=\tfrac{s^3}{27}$, so $A^2\le\tfrac{s^4}{27}$ and $A\le\tfrac{s^2}{3\sqrt3}$. Equality needs $x=y=z$, i.e. $a=b=c$.

blocks.title: Extremal positions
blocks.body:
Many problems ask for the position that makes a quantity smallest. Two ideas solve a large share of them.

Reflection. To find the shortest path from $P$ to a line $\ell$ and on to $Q$ (both on the same side of $\ell$), reflect $Q$ in $\ell$ to $Q'$. Any path $P\to X\to Q$ with $X\in\ell$ has the same length as $P\to X\to Q'$, which is at least $PQ'$, with equality when $X$ is on segment $PQ'$. The optimal path makes equal angles with $\ell$, as a light ray does.

Rotation. The point $P$ minimising $PA+PB+PC$ in a triangle with all angles below $120^\circ$ is the Fermat point, from which each side is seen at $120^\circ$. The idea of the proof: rotate the plane by $60^\circ$ about $B$, sending $A$ to $A'$ and $P$ to $P'$. Triangle $BPP'$ is equilateral, so $PB=PP'$, and $PA=P'A'$. Hence $PA+PB+PC=A'P'+P'P+PC\ge A'C$, a fixed length, with equality when $A',P',P,C$ lie on a line in that order. (We do not carry out the check that this happens exactly at the Fermat point.)

In both cases the method is the same: transform the figure so that the quantity to minimise becomes the length of a broken line between two fixed points, then use the triangle inequality.

blocks.title: Distances to the vertices
blocks.body: Let $P$ be a point inside triangle $ABC$. Prove that $s< PA+PB+PC< a+b+c$.
blocks.solution:
Lower bound: by the triangle inequality $PA+PB>c$, $PB+PC>a$, $PC+PA>b$ (strict, since $P$ is not on a side). Adding, $2(PA+PB+PC)>a+b+c=2s$.

Upper bound: extend $BP$ to meet $AC$ at $Q$. Then $PC< PQ+QC$, so $PB+PC< PB+PQ+QC=BQ+QC$, and $BQ< BA+AQ$, so $BQ+QC< BA+AQ+QC=c+b$. Thus $PB+PC< b+c$; similarly $PC+PA< c+a$ and $PA+PB< a+b$. Adding gives $2(PA+PB+PC)<2(a+b+c)$.

blocks.title: A shortest perimeter
blocks.body: An angle with vertex $O$ and sides $OA$, $OB$ has measure $\theta<90^\circ$, and $P$ is a point inside it. Find the smallest possible perimeter of a triangle $PXY$ with $X$ on ray $OA$ and $Y$ on ray $OB$.
blocks.solution:
Reflect $P$ in line $OA$ to $P_1$ and in line $OB$ to $P_2$. Then $PX=P_1X$ and $PY=P_2Y$, so the perimeter is $P_1X+XY+YP_2\ge P_1P_2$.

The reflections give $OP_1=OP_2=OP$ and $\angle P_1OP_2=2\angle AOP+2\angle POB=2\theta<180^\circ$. The rays from $O$ occur in the order $OP_1,OA,OP,OB,OP_2$ inside this angle, so the segment $P_1P_2$ crosses ray $OA$ and then ray $OB$; choosing $X,Y$ at these crossings achieves equality. The triangle $OP_1P_2$ is isosceles with apex angle $2\theta$, so the minimum is

$$P_1P_2=2\,OP\sin\theta.$$

For example, with $\theta=30^\circ$ the smallest perimeter equals $OP$, whatever the direction of $P$ inside the angle.

blocks.title: Perimeter versus inradius
blocks.body: Prove that every triangle satisfies $s\ge3\sqrt3\,r$, with equality only for the equilateral triangle. Deduce that a triangle of perimeter $L$ has inradius at most $\dfrac{L}{6\sqrt3}$.
blocks.solution:
Combine $A=rs$ with the isoperimetric inequality for triangles, $A\le\tfrac{s^2}{3\sqrt3}$: we get $rs\le\tfrac{s^2}{3\sqrt3}$, so $s\ge3\sqrt3\,r$. Equality requires equality in the isoperimetric bound, i.e. an equilateral triangle. With $L=2s$ this reads $r\le\tfrac{s}{3\sqrt3}=\tfrac{L}{6\sqrt3}$.

Check with the equilateral triangle of side $1$: $s=\tfrac32$ and $r=\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3}$, so $3\sqrt3\,r=\tfrac32=s$.

blocks.title: A product version
blocks.body: With $P$, $D,E,F$ as in the Erdős–Mordell inequality, prove that $PA\cdot PB\cdot PC\ge8\,PD\cdot PE\cdot PF$.
blocks.solution:
Use the three inequalities from Steps 1 and 2 of the proof, followed by AM–GM on each:

$$PA\ge\frac caPE+\frac baPF\ge\frac2a\sqrt{bc\cdot PE\cdot PF},\qquad PB\ge\frac cbPD+\frac abPF\ge\frac2b\sqrt{ca\cdot PD\cdot PF},$$

$$PC\ge\frac bcPD+\frac acPE\ge\frac2c\sqrt{ab\cdot PD\cdot PE}.$$

All quantities are nonnegative, so we may multiply:

$$PA\cdot PB\cdot PC\ge\frac{8}{abc}\sqrt{a^2b^2c^2\,(PD\cdot PE\cdot PF)^2}=8\,PD\cdot PE\cdot PF.$$

The side lengths cancel completely, which is the point of pairing each distance with the right side in the lemma. Equality again occurs for the centre of an equilateral triangle.

blocks.body:
- Checking the equilateral triangle is not a proof. It only tells you where equality might be, which is useful for planning the AM–GM steps.
- Hypotheses on position matter. Erdős–Mordell can fail for points outside the triangle, and the Fermat point description needs all angles below $120^\circ$.
- Equality cases must be consistent: if a proof chains several inequalities, equality in the result needs equality in every step at the same time.
- The isoperimetric inequality compares area with the square of the perimeter. A shape with larger perimeter can have smaller area, so "more fence, more field" is false without fixing the shape.
- The Ravi substitution with $x,y,z>0$ covers nondegenerate triangles only. If a problem allows degenerate triangles, treat the cases $x=0$, $y=0$ or $z=0$ separately.

The algebra behind these proofs is [[amgm]] and, for angle inequalities, [[convexity|Jensen's inequality]]: for example concavity of $\sin$ on $[0,\pi]$ gives $\sin A+\sin B+\sin C\le\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}$. After the Ravi substitution many triangle inequalities become [[symmetric-ineq|symmetric polynomial inequalities]], and [[cauchy-schwarz]] handles sums of ratios. Euler's formula $OI^2=R(R-2r)$ belongs to [[triangle-centres]], and coordinate proofs of geometric inequalities use the frames of [[analytic-geometry]]. Hurwitz's proof of $4\pi A\le L^2$ expands the boundary curve in [[fourier-poisson|Fourier series]], while polygon versions with fixed perimeter are natural exercises in [[lagrange-multipliers]]. Extremal questions about many points in the plane lead to [[discrete-geometry]], and the isoperimetric inequality itself is the prototype of a large part of geometric analysis.

1. Prove that the altitudes of every triangle satisfy $h_a+h_b+h_c\ge9r$.
2. Show that among all rectangles of perimeter $L$ the square has the largest area, and compare its value of $L^2/A$ with $4\pi$.
3. Take an equilateral triangle and a point $P$ outside it, below the midpoint of one side. Find a position of $P$ for which $PA+PB+PC<2(PD+PE+PF)$.
4. Prove that the regular $n$-gon has $L^2/A=4n\tan(\pi/n)$ and that this quantity decreases as $n$ increases.
